hints: Look carefully at the centre of the vein in the micrograph. Notice the difference between the tiny, tightly packed cells in the middle and the much larger, open tubes around them.
Remember which vascular tissue carries sugars by mass flow, and which helper cells next to it use ATP and proton (H+) pumps to load sucrose by co-transport.
walkthrough:
**Orientate yourself in the micrograph**

Look at this leaf in cross-section. You can see palisade cells at the top, spongy cells below, and a round vascular bundle (the vein) in the middle. That vein contains both xylem and phloem.

**Recall what proton pumps do in mass flow**

Mass flow is translocation of sucrose in phloem. At a source like a leaf, sucrose is actively loaded. Companion cells pump out protons (H+) using ATP, then let H+ flow back in together with sucrose by co-transport. That sucrose then moves into the sieve tube.

**Identify the phloem in the vein**

In a leaf vein, xylem is made of large, wide, empty vessels for water support. Phloem is made of much smaller, densely packed sieve tubes and companion cells, usually grouped together in the centre of the bundle. Label C points exactly to that central cluster of tiny cells, so it is the site of proton-pump loading for mass flow.

options.A: This points to the outer bundle sheath around the vein, which controls movement into the vascular tissue but does not use proton pumps for phloem loading.
options.B: This points to the larger vessels of the xylem, which transport water by cohesion-tension and transpiration pull, not by proton pumps and mass flow.
options.C: This is the phloem with companion cells and sieve tubes. Companion cells use proton pumps to load sucrose for mass flow translocation.
options.D: This points to the lower epidermis of the leaf, which protects the leaf and contains stomata, but plays no direct role in proton-pump loading for mass flow.
